title: Clarifying Requirements
objectives: Ask the questions that change the design
State assumptions when answers are vague

cards.title: Functional first
cards.body: Ask what users do: the three or four core actions, such as post, follow and view the feed. Say out loud what is out of scope.

cards.title: Non-functional next
cards.body: Scale (users, QPS, data), latency targets, availability, consistency needs and the read/write ratio. These shape the architecture more than features do.

cards.title: Five clarifying minutes
cards.body: 5 steps from “Who are the users and what do they do?” to “State assumptions out loud”, via “Which features are core and which are later?”.
steps: Who are the users and what do they do?
Which features are core and which are later?

cards.title: India-scale anchors
cards.body: Useful anchors: about 900M internet users, UPI in the tens of billions of transactions a month, IPL streams with tens of millions of concurrent viewers. Use them to sanity-check numbers.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Asking twenty questions without stating assumptions, or asking none. Ask what changes the design, then say “I’ll assume X; tell me if that is off.”

questions.prompt: For “Design Instagram”, which is a functional requirement?

choices.label: 500M daily users
Feed p99 latency under 200 ms
Users can post photos and follow others
99.95% availability

questions.prompt: Which question uncovers a non-functional requirement?

choices.label: Do we support stories that expire after a day?
Can users tag friends in their photo posts?
How quickly must a new post appear in followers’ feeds?
Can users add filters to photos before posting?

questions.prompt: Order the clarifying minutes.

items.label: Who are the users and what do they do?

questions.prompt: The interviewer shrugs at “how many users?”. Best move?

choices.label: State an assumption, such as 100M daily users, and continue
Refuse to continue until you are given a number
Skip the estimation step entirely and move on
Design for unlimited scale just to be safe

questions.explanation: Assumptions keep you moving and can be corrected.

questions.prompt: UPI handles about 15B transactions a month. Roughly what is the average per second?
questions.formula: A month is about 2.6M seconds; 15B ÷ 2.6M ≈ 5,800 per second.
questions.workedAnswer: A month is about 2.6M seconds; 15B ÷ 2.6M ≈ 5,800 per second.
questions.explanation: A month is about 2.6M seconds; 15B ÷ 2.6M ≈ 5,800 per second.

flashcards.front: For “Design Instagram”, which is a functional requirement?
flashcards.back: Users can post photos and follow others. Functional = what users can do.

flashcards.front: Which question uncovers a non-functional requirement?
flashcards.back: How quickly must a new post appear in followers’ feeds?. Freshness is a latency/consistency requirement.

flashcards.front: The interviewer shrugs at “how many users?”. Best move?
flashcards.back: State an assumption, such as 100M daily users, and continue. Assumptions keep you moving and can be corrected.

title: Deep Dives & Trade-off Language
objectives: Choose the part of the design worth a deep dive
Phrase trade-offs with requirement, cost and mitigation

cards.title: Choosing the deep dive
cards.body: Pick the part most likely to break at your numbers: the hot key, the write path, the fan-out. Or ask which part the interviewer wants. Go deep on one, not shallow on five.

cards.title: Trade-off sentences
cards.body: Use: “A or B. I choose A because requirement X; the cost is Y; I’ll mitigate with Z.” It shows judgement instead of memorised answers.

cards.title: A deep dive
cards.body: 5 steps from “Name the risk with a number” to “Say how you would monitor it”, via “Show how the design fails”.
steps: Name the risk with a number
Pick one and name its cost
Say how you would monitor it

cards.title: Soften absolutes
cards.body: Avoid “always” and “never”. Say “for this read-heavy feed I’d cache with a short TTL”, not “caching is always right”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Presenting one option as obviously correct with no downside. Interviewers push back until you name the cost; naming it first earns the point.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest trade-off statement?

choices.label: Async replication, because it is always faster and always better for every workload
Async replication, because writes must be fast; we may lose seconds on failover, so payments use a sync path
Kafka, because it is the industry standard that most large companies already use
Either works here; the choice does not really matter for this design at all

questions.prompt: Order the trade-off sentence.
questions.explanation: The cost and mitigation are what interviewers listen for.

questions.prompt: URL shortener at 100K redirects/s. Best deep-dive choice?

choices.label: Which logging library the service uses
The signup page and its form validation
The redirect read path and caching of hot links
The admin dashboard for managing links

questions.prompt: Which sentence is best in an interview?

choices.label: Caching is always the right answer
Microservices always beat monoliths
For this read-heavy feed, I’d cache with a short TTL
Never use SQL at scale

questions.prompt: Order a deep dive.

items.label: Name the risk with a number

title: Common Mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common design-interview mistakes
Keep designs proportional to the numbers

cards.title: Designing before scoping
cards.body: Drawing boxes before knowing scale or features. Everything after rests on guesses.

cards.title: Over-engineering
cards.body: Kafka, microservices and sharding for 1,000 users. Start simple and add components when a number forces you.

cards.title: Unused numbers
cards.body: Estimating, then never using the estimate. If you computed 50K QPS, say what it means for caching and the database.

cards.title: Recovering from a stall
cards.body: 5 steps from “Notice you are stuck” to “Note it for a later deep dive”, via “Say what you are weighing”.
steps: Pick a simple option and move on
Note it for a later deep dive

cards.title: Silent thinking
cards.body: Long silences leave the interviewer guessing. Think aloud, check in (“should I go deeper here?”) and accept hints.

questions.prompt: At 1,000 daily users, which design is reasonable?

choices.label: Sharded Cassandra across three regions
Kubernetes with a service mesh
Kafka plus twelve microservices
One app server and one managed database, with backups

questions.prompt: You estimated 50K read QPS. What should follow?

choices.label: Use it: say a cache is needed and roughly how many app servers
Move on: estimation is just a phase to get through
Re-estimate it more precisely with exact figures
Ask whether 50K is right and stop there

questions.prompt: You are stuck on the database choice. Best move?

choices.label: Stay silent until you are completely sure of the answer
Think aloud about the options and check in with the interviewer
Switch to talking about the frontend to fill the time
Pick one quickly without explaining why you chose it

questions.explanation: Reasoning out loud earns credit even when unsure.

questions.prompt: Order a recovery from a stall.

items.label: Note it for a deep dive

questions.explanation: Keep moving, flag it, return later.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign you skipped scoping?

choices.label: Early on, you asked about the read/write ratio
Early on, you asked what is out of scope for now
You stated your traffic assumptions out loud
Halfway through, you learn the system only needs 10 writes a day

questions.explanation: The design was built on guesses.

title: Communication in the Interview
objectives: Grow a design step by step from the numbers

cards.title: Narrate the design
cards.body: Say what you are drawing and why: “Reads dominate, so I’m putting a cache here.” The interviewer grades reasoning they can hear.

cards.title: Evolve, don’t jump
cards.body: Start with the simplest design that works, then add a component each time a number forces you: one server, then a load balancer, cache, replicas, shards.

cards.title: Growing a design aloud
cards.body: 5 steps from “One server” to “Add shards and regions”, via “Add a load balancer and stateless apps”.
steps: Add a load balancer and stateless apps

cards.title: Work with the interviewer
cards.body: Check in at transitions (“requirements look settled; shall I estimate?”). Treat hints as help, and if you do not know a tool, describe the property you need.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Arguing with a hint or bluffing about a technology. Say “I haven’t used X, but I need a store with property Y” instead.

questions.prompt: Which is good narration?

choices.label: This is how Netflix does it, so we will copy that design
Now I’ll add a box here, and then another box over here
Reads are 100× writes, so I’ll put a cache in front of the database
I’ll add Redis here because Redis is what everyone uses

questions.prompt: You do not know a database the interviewer mentions. Best move?

choices.label: Refuse to use it and insist on your own
Change the subject to a database you know
Say so, and describe the properties you need from it
Pretend you know it and keep talking

questions.prompt: At 1K users, what should your first diagram be?

choices.label: The final multi-region design
Microservices with Kafka
A sharded cluster
One server and a database

questions.prompt: Order the growth of a design.
questions.explanation: Each step answers a specific bottleneck.

questions.prompt: When is a good time to check in with the interviewer?

choices.label: At transitions, such as after requirements and before the deep dive
After every sentence, to be sure they agree
Only at the very end, once the design is done
Never: checking in makes you look unsure

flashcards.front: Which is good narration?
flashcards.back: Reads are 100× writes, so I’ll put a cache in front of the database. Decision plus reason.

flashcards.front: You do not know a database the interviewer mentions. Best move?
flashcards.back: Say so, and describe the properties you need from it. Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.

flashcards.front: At 1K users, what should your first diagram be?
flashcards.back: One server and a database. Start simple, then grow.

flashcards.front: When is a good time to check in with the interviewer?
flashcards.back: At transitions, such as after requirements and before the deep dive. Natural break points.

title: Numbers & Latency Cheat Sheet
objectives: Recall the latency ladder by order of magnitude
Convert daily volumes to per-second rates
Size a server fleet from peak QPS

cards.title: Latency ladder
cards.body: Memory read: about 100 ns. SSD random read: about 100 µs. Same-datacentre round trip: about 0.5 ms. Disk seek: about 10 ms. Mumbai to Singapore: about 60 ms. India to US East: about 200 ms.

cards.title: Throughput anchors
cards.body: A tuned app server handles roughly 1–10K simple requests/s; a single Postgres primary a few thousand writes/s; Redis around 100K operations/s per node. Rough, but enough to size a fleet.

cards.title: Powers of ten
cards.body: A day is 86,400 s, about 10^5. A million a day is about 12 a second; a billion a day is about 12K a second. A million 1 KB records is about 1 GB; a million 1 MB files is about 1 TB.

cards.title: Sizing a fleet
cards.body: 5 steps from “Peak QPS from the estimate” to “Add N+1 for failures”, via “Per-server capacity from the anchors”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Quoting numbers to three significant figures. Interviewers want orders of magnitude and stated assumptions, not false precision.

questions.prompt: Which is fastest?

choices.label: A disk seek
A same-datacentre round trip
Reading from memory
An SSD random read

questions.explanation: 100 ns versus 0.5 ms, 100 µs and 10 ms.

A billion requests a day is roughly how many per second?
Order the fleet-sizing steps.
questions.explanation: Headroom and spare capacity come last.

questions.prompt: A round trip from India to US East is about:

choices.label: 200 ms
2 ms
2 s
20 ms

questions.explanation: Distance sets a floor that caching cannot remove.

flashcards.front: Which is fastest?
flashcards.back: Reading from memory. 100 ns versus 0.5 ms, 100 µs and 10 ms.

flashcards.front: A billion requests a day is roughly how many per second?
A round trip from India to US East is about:
flashcards.back: 200 ms. Distance sets a floor that caching cannot remove.

title: Pattern-to-Use-Case Map
objectives: Map workload shapes to standard patterns
Pick patterns for read-heavy, write-heavy, real-time and correctness-first features
Link each pattern back to its lesson

cards.title: Read-heavy
cards.body: Cache-aside, a CDN for static files and media, read replicas. Examples: product pages, news feeds, URL redirects.

cards.title: Write-heavy and spiky
cards.body: Queues to absorb bursts, batching, LSM or wide-column stores, sharding by a high-cardinality key. Examples: logging, IoT, clickstreams.

cards.title: Real-time
cards.body: WebSockets or SSE through gateways, pub/sub to route messages, presence in Redis. Examples: chat, live scores, ride tracking.

cards.title: Correctness first
cards.body: Transactions, idempotency keys, sagas, strong consistency on the hot rows. Examples: payments, bookings, inventory.

cards.title: Search and nearby
cards.body: An inverted index for text, geohash or a quadtree for location, both fed from the primary database by CDC. Examples: product search, restaurants near me.

questions.prompt: A live cricket score goes to 20M phones. Which patterns?

choices.label: SSE or WebSockets through gateways, with pub/sub fan-out
Every phone polling the database each second
A strongly consistent transaction per update
A nightly batch export

questions.prompt: Ticket booking for a concert. Which pattern matters most?

choices.label: Transactions and idempotency on seat holds
Caching seat availability at the CDN for an hour
Fan-out on write
Eventual consistency on seat counts

questions.explanation: Double-selling a seat is the failure to avoid.

questions.prompt: IoT sensors write 1M points a second. Which patterns?

choices.label: A queue to absorb bursts, then a write-optimised store sharded by device
One Postgres primary with many indexes on the readings table
Strongly consistent writes replicated across several regions
An inverted index over the sensor readings, like a search engine

questions.prompt: Restaurants within 2 km. Which pattern?

choices.label: An LRU cache alone
A full-text inverted index
Kafka partitions by city
A geohash or quadtree index

questions.prompt: URL redirects at 100K per second.

approaches.label: Cache-aside plus CDN or edge caching
approaches.description: Serve hot links from memory near users

rationaleOptions.label: Edge caching cuts latency for distant users
Reads dwarf writes and links rarely change

rationaleConflicts.r3: Redirects are reads; write-behind only changes how writes are stored.

questions.explanation: Read-heavy, rarely changing: cache close to users.

flashcards.back: SSE or WebSockets through gateways, with pub/sub fan-out. Push through gateways.
